newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Aztech enters digital photo market.
newsitem.headline: Aztech enters digital photo market.

text.p: Multimedia company Aztech Systems Ltd said on Tuesday it was entering the photography market with the launch of its Desktop Photo Developer (DPD).
The DPD develops photographs taken with a digital camera through the use of a technology named Cylithography licensed from U.S. company Cycolor Inc.
The technology produces photosensitive polyester film which contains light-sensitive microcapsules.
Digital photos can be produced as and when required even when the film cartridge is not completely used.

Michael Mun, president of Aztech told reporters at a products preview the photography market was valued at US$3.0 bilion and moving towards digital photography as prices drop and the market realised the advantages of instant editing, output and transmission over communications networks.
He said more than three million digital cameras were expected to be sold worldwide this year.
Aztech aimed to "build capacity for one million units in the first 12 months," Mun said.
It expected to have its first mass shipment by the second quarter of 1997, he said.
Mun said the company would target the U.S. and European markets first but saw demand in Asia-Pacific countries like Japan, Hong Kong, South Korea and Australia as well.
Aztech's DPD would be sold mainly through partnerships and to original equipment manufacturers, he said.
Aztech has two models of the DPD -- an internal one which fits into the 5.25 inch disk drive bay of a personal computer and an external one.
Its DPD will initially print 3R photos and will have models to produce larger sized photos later on.

On other product areas, Mun said Aztech was moving to faster speed 56 kbps modem and 56kbps audio telephony boards to allow users to access information on the Internet at twice the speeds currently achievable using normal telephone lines.
Aztech audio telephony boards provide fax, auto answering machine, speaker phones and modem features integrated with its 3D sound technology.
But Aztech was not rushing into the Digital Video Disc (DVD) business, said Mun.

"DVD is for entertainment. For the PC industry, they don't really need that kind of quality now. Especially with the higher-speed and higher performance CD-ROMs is there really an urgent need for higher performance?," he said.
He said Aztech was watching the recordable CD (CDR) market.
"We believe there is an opportunity for CDR," he said, especially when prices in CDR drops to about twice that of CD-ROMs.
